name: Polystyrene-eating worm farm
subtitle: farmed insects that digest foam packaging

effects.effect: the bacteria in the gut steer the body's immunity, weight and mood
bacteria found at a recycling plant make an enzyme that breaks PET plastic apart

effect: the bacteria in the gut steer the body's immunity, weight and mood
how: Polystyrene foam is bulky, worth nothing to a recycler and lasts for centuries, so nearly all of it is buried. Mealworms already nibble it, slowly, because a few of their gut bacteria can crack the chains; give those bacteria a written-to-order set of genes from the plastic-eating family and the worms get a gut that takes the foam apart in days. The fattened larvae are themselves protein for fish and poultry feed.
obstacle: Flame retardants and heavy metals from the foam could end up in the larvae, and so in the food chain, unless they can be shown to pass straight through.
why: Turns the most worthless plastic into animal feed using an animal already doing it slowly.
real: Mealworms living on polystyrene and the causal role of their gut bacteria are well demonstrated (Exiguobacterium sp. YT2, Klebsiella sp. WJ2020 at 4.35% and Cellulosimicrobium at 6.93% film loss over 60 days), but no engineered gut symbiont carrying added plastic-degrading genes, and no feed-safety demonstration, was found.
